content.text: Like regular optionals, implicitly unwrapped optionals might contain a value or they might be `nil`. However, unlike regular optionals you don’t need to unwrap them in order to use them: you can use them as if they weren’t optional at all.
Implicitly unwrapped optionals are created by adding an exclamation mark after your type name, like this:

Because they behave as if they were already unwrapped, you don’t need `if let` or `guard let` to use implicitly unwrapped optionals. However, if you try to use them and they have no value – if they are `nil` – your code crashes.

Implicitly unwrapped optionals exist because sometimes a variable will start life as nil, but will always have a value before you need to use it. Because you know they will have a value by the time you need them, it’s helpful not having to write `if let` all the time.
That being said, if you’re able to use regular optionals instead it’s generally a good idea.

title: Implicitly unwrapped optionals
question: Which of these are true about optionals?
hint: Both `String?` and `String!` might have a value or might not.

correct.answer: Optionals allow us to represent the absence of a value.
correct.reason: They can store a regular value for their type or nil.

correct.answer: A `String?` must be unwrapped before use.
A `String!` does not need to be unwrapped before use.
correct.reason: If you access an implicitly unwrapped optional while it contains nil, your code will crash.

correct.answer: Swift uses `nil` to represent the absence of a value.
You can use `if let` or `guard let` to unwrap optionals.
If you try to use an implicitly unwrapped optional when it is `nil`, your code crashes.

wrong.reason: Although they are both optional, the former requires unwrapping before use whereas the latter does not.

wrong.answer: You shouldn't pass optionals into functions
wrong.reason: You can do so if you wish; there's no reason not to.

wrong.answer: You can't use both `String!` and `String?` in the same program.
wrong.reason: You can mix and match these all you need.

wrong.answer: Once an optional has a value, you can't set it back to `nil`.
wrong.reason: You can set an optional back to nil whenever you want.
